strengths: The paper targets a meaningful and underexplored capability: reading information-dense, high-resolution transit maps and converting visual evidence into structured routes. The use of 30 cities across 13 countries and four languages provides useful geographic and visual diversity.
The benchmark construction combines map metadata, routes retrieved from map services, and manual verification. Separating route feasibility from route quality is a sensible evaluation goal.

The empirical study covers 15 contemporary open- and closed-source MLLMs. Reporting short/long questions, output lengths, text-only controls, difficulty and city breakdowns, and qualitative failures provides several useful views of current model behavior.

The results demonstrate substantial remaining headroom: even the strongest evaluated model reaches only 63.02% and 59.11% weighted accuracy on short and long questions, respectively. Examples of visual confusion, formatting failures, hallucination, and refusal are informative.
weaknesses: The proposed map score is not technically well-defined as presented. Algorithm 2 uses alternative operations written as divisions (for example, min(10, score)/min(20, score) and +10/+20), does not define how unequal numbers of predicted and reference segments are paired, and can divide by zero when both routes have zero via stops or when both via-stop sets are empty. These are common cases, such as adjacent stations. Because this score is a central contribution and all map-score results depend on its implementation, this is a material correctness and reproducibility problem rather than a presentation refinement.

The central claim that open-source base models outperform reasoning models while the opposite holds for closed-source models is not supported by controlled comparisons. Only Kimi provides a clearly paired open-source base/reasoning comparison; the other models differ in architecture, size, and training. On the closed-source side, Gemini-2.5-Flash has lower long-question accuracy than GPT-4o, and Doubao-428 does not outperform Doubao-115. The paper itself acknowledges that the comparison is potentially unfair, but nevertheless presents a broad causal explanation involving reinforcement learning and knowledge coverage.

Route-quality ground truth is incomplete and service-dependent. Google Maps and Gaode return selected contemporary alternatives rather than all equally optimal routes, while the manuscript does not define optimality precisely or report how many references are available per query. A feasible and equally efficient route absent from those API results can therefore receive a low score merely because its segments do not exactly align with a retrieved reference.

The benchmark is narrower than the framing suggests: it contains only 30 underlying images and three rigid templates for essentially one route-finding task. The test set contains 312 instances from 11 cities, including only 23 hard questions and one hard-middle example. This limits the reliability of conclusions about fine-grained visual reasoning broadly.

The evaluation reports only an author-designed weighted metric with subjective map-difficulty labels and fixed, unvalidated weights. It provides neither ordinary unweighted accuracy nor confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests. Several buckets and cities have very small sample counts, so claims about difficulty, scaling, and correlations are not adequately quantified.

Dataset construction and verification lack important details: the number and expertise of annotators, independent verification or agreement, criteria for manual map difficulty, test-set selection procedure, and audit/error rates are not reported. The meaning of dataset size is also inconsistent: the paper calls 1,008 the number of question-answer pairs, while each instance appears to produce both a short and a long question and Table 1 denotes 1,008 ×2.

Reproduction of the model results is underspecified. The paper relies on default API settings and official Hugging Face configurations without giving exact model/API versions, decoding parameters, evaluation dates, random seeds, or the actual pixel/token preprocessing applied to each high-resolution map. Appendix D summarizes model architectures but does not specify the experimental input transformations.

The correctness evaluator verifies endpoints, line membership, and transfer continuity but not explicitly whether the stated within-line traversal is connected on maps with branches or whether the predicted sequence represents an actual service path. Moreover, strict parsing assigns zero to potentially correct answers with minor formatting deviations, conflating visual-route reasoning with instruction-format compliance without reporting those failure rates separately.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant and challenging capability: extracting and reasoning over fine-grained information in high-resolution transit maps. This complements benchmarks based on synthetic diagrams or tool-assisted geographic reasoning.

REASONMAP covers 30 cities in 13 countries, includes multilingual station names, and uses manually checked map metadata and routes. Holding out 11 cities for the 312-sample test set provides some geographic separation from the training data.
The evaluation spans 15 open- and closed-source MLLMs, reports short- and long-answer results, token usage, difficulty and city breakdowns, and representative failure cases.
The text-only control is informative: the substantial drops for stronger models provide evidence that visual inputs contribute beyond memorized transit knowledge.
weaknesses: The correctness metric has a consequential validity flaw. Algorithm 1 checks endpoints, line membership, and transfer consistency, but neither verifies the requested optimality nor evaluates the via-stop counts/lists required by long questions. Thus an unnecessarily long route can be marked correct, and a long answer with entirely wrong intermediate-stop content can receive full accuracy. This undermines the principal accuracy results.

The proposed map score is ad hoc and insufficiently specified. Segment-pair alignment is undefined when predicted and reference routes have different numbers of segments; the pseudocode ambiguously combines short- and long-question formulas; and the caps, component weights, and correctness bonuses lack validation against human judgments of route quality. Consequently, it is unclear that score differences measure meaningful efficiency or answer quality.

The headline conclusion that open-source reasoning models underperform base models while the reverse holds for closed models is not supported by controlled comparisons. Most models differ simultaneously in architecture, scale, training data, image processing, and inference configuration; only a limited subset forms matched base/reasoning pairs. Closed APIs also use unspecified defaults, and the paper itself acknowledges that the comparison is potentially unfair.

Inference conditions may systematically disadvantage reasoning models: open models are capped at 2,048 output tokens, while reasoning models produce much longer responses and closed models follow unrelated API defaults. No truncation or format-failure rates, repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity analyses are reported, despite strict parsing and stochastic APIs potentially affecting the rankings.

The benchmark has narrow task diversity: all examples instantiate one origin-to-destination routing task through only three rigid templates, with short and long questions largely differing in required output detail. Claims about fine-grained visual reasoning in general therefore exceed the demonstrated scope.

Dataset difficulty and evaluation sampling are weakly justified. Map difficulty is assigned manually without annotation protocol or agreement; the intended 20:15:5 per-map distribution is not achieved; only 23 of 312 test examples are hard, including a difficulty bucket containing one sample; and arbitrary difficulty weights amplify these small, unstable groups.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. Exact prompts and templates are given, but API evaluation dates or immutable model versions, decoding parameters, parsing implementation details, and model-specific image preprocessing at inference are not fully documented. The paper says copyrighted maps will not be redistributed and supplies source links rather than preserved inputs, making exact future reconstruction uncertain.

Several analyses are speculative rather than experimentally established, including attributing city-level differences to prominence/language and reasoning-model behavior to reinforcement learning. Counterfactual station-name tests, OCR or graph-search baselines, and controlled ablations would be needed to separate visual perception, prior knowledge, route planning, and formatting failures.

strengths: REASONMAP targets an important and underexplored capability: extracting and reasoning over fine-grained information in high-resolution, information-dense transit maps. This is relevant to computer vision because success requires text recognition, visual tracing, spatial reasoning, and multimodal integration rather than ordinary image-level recognition.

The dataset has useful geographic, linguistic, and visual diversity, covering 30 cities in 13 countries. The construction pipeline combines map-service routes with manual correction and verification, and the separation of map difficulty from route/question difficulty is thoughtful.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, evaluating 15 open- and closed-source MLLMs. Reporting short- and long-answer performance, token usage, text-only controls, difficulty breakdowns, city-level results, and qualitative failure cases provides a more informative characterization than a single aggregate leaderboard.

The text-only ablation is particularly valuable: the substantial drops for stronger models provide evidence that visual input matters, while the small or reversed changes for some weaker models expose reliance on memorized transit knowledge or textual priors.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, includes explicit prompt templates and evaluation pseudocode, discusses high-resolution preprocessing, and acknowledges limits on generalizing beyond transit diagrams.
weaknesses: The headline conclusion that open-source base models outperform reasoning models while the reverse holds for closed-source models is not adequately controlled. Most comparisons involve different architectures, sizes, training data, and image-processing pipelines rather than matched base/reasoning variants. Even within the closed-source Doubao family, one reasoning model underperforms the base model on several measures. The paper should present this as an observation about the tested systems, not evidence about reasoning training generally.

Inference conditions materially disadvantage some open-source reasoning models: they are capped at 2,048 output tokens, whereas closed-source models use provider defaults and OpenAI o3 averages 2,372 tokens on long questions. Several open reasoning models already average 1,287–1,619 tokens, so truncation and reduced space for the required final format are plausible confounders. No truncation rates, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or sensitivity analysis are reported.

The correctness evaluator checks endpoint membership, line validity, and transfer consistency, but does not explicitly verify traversal connectivity/order on branched or direction-dependent lines. The map score is also hand-designed, uses unclear segment pairing when predicted and reference routes differ in length, and mixes reference similarity with a large correctness bonus. There is no validation showing that this metric agrees with human judgments of route quality or is robust to equivalent routes.

The effective benchmark test is only 312 origin-destination pairs over 11 maps, with just 23 hard questions; one reported difficulty bucket contains a single example and consequently attains 100% accuracy. The arbitrary difficulty weights amplify sparse buckets, yet unweighted results, uncertainty estimates, and statistical tests are absent. This weakens claims about scaling, difficulty trends, and differences between models.

Dataset quality assurance is underspecified. The manuscript says samples are human verified but does not report the number or expertise of annotators, independent verification, agreement, error rates, or a systematic audit of routes obtained from potentially changing map-service APIs. Map difficulty is manually assigned without an operational rubric.

Reproducibility is uncertain because the exact transit images are apparently not redistributed, only source links are provided, and online maps can change or disappear. API versions/dates and important generation settings for closed models are not fully recorded. The split also appears to divide questions rather than holding out maps, which would permit strong leakage if the provided training set is used for model development.

Some analysis is speculative: explanations involving reinforcement learning, knowledge breadth, city prominence, and visual integration are offered without controlled evidence. There are also internal inconsistencies in the appendix case discussion about which model identifies Augustins as belonging to which line. These are mainly presentation/interpretation issues, but they reduce confidence in the broader conclusions.

strengths: REASONMAP targets a meaningful and underexplored combination of fine-grained perception, visual grounding, and route planning over information-dense transit maps. The 30-city, 13-country collection offers useful geographic, linguistic, and diagram-style diversity.

The benchmark construction is reasonably systematic: station and line extraction is manually corrected, routes are checked for visual traceability, three annotators perform quality control, and train/test cities are disjoint.

The evaluation includes complementary signals: strict route feasibility, partial-credit route quality, short and long question variants, difficulty annotations, visual-masking experiments, symbolic-map experiments, and component-level error analysis.

The evaluation of 16 MLLMs establishes useful reference results and shows that the task remains challenging even for strong proprietary models. The cross-city reinforcement-fine-tuning baseline also demonstrates that the dataset can support training research.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, and the appendix provides question templates, map sources, preprocessing information, evaluation pseudocode, difficulty buckets, and qualitative cases.
weaknesses: The headline conclusion that reasoning models underperform base models in open-source settings but outperform them in closed-source settings is not supported by controlled comparisons. Kimi is the only clear matched open-source base/reasoning pair, while the other models differ in family, scale, training data, release generation, image preprocessing, and inference interface. The closed-source comparison is similarly confounded, as the paper itself briefly acknowledges. Consequently, the claimed explanation involving visual grounding and self-correction is largely based on selected cases rather than causal evidence.

The correctness metric does not enforce the requested optimality. It only checks endpoints, line membership, and transfer consistency, so an unnecessarily long but feasible detour can be counted as correct; the appendix explicitly describes such a route as functionally correct but suboptimal. Moreover, checking that two stops belong to a line may be insufficient for branched services unless connectivity and branch direction are explicitly represented and validated, which Algorithm 1 does not show.

The map-score specification has important ambiguities and apparent edge cases. Algorithm 2 divides the via-stop error by the maximum of predicted and reference counts and computes an IoU over via-stop sets, both of which are undefined when the corresponding counts or union are zero—a common case for direct routes. Segment pairing when prediction and reference contain different numbers of segments is also unspecified. These omissions affect both technical confidence and independent reproducibility of the core metric.

The empirical test set contains only 312 route queries over 11 distinct map images, with highly uneven bucket sizes—for example, one hard/medium sample. Repeated questions over the same image are correlated, yet results are presented without uncertainty estimates, repeated inference, or per-map aggregation. The custom difficulty weighting is arbitrary and no sensitivity analysis is provided for those weights, although weighted accuracy is the principal reported metric.

The GRPO baseline is insufficiently specified for reproduction: the paper omits training duration or update count, reward-component weights and exact values, image/token settings, decoding parameters, seeds, and compute details. Its stated GRPO objective is also a simplified centered-reward policy-gradient expression that does not document clipping or how the reported KL coefficient enters optimization.

Some analyses overreach their evidence. The conclusion that failures are primarily grounding and spatial reasoning is based mainly on a few qualitative examples and cross-benchmark OCR scores collected from technical reports under potentially different settings. The language ablation covers only two Chinese cities and substitutes unrelated New York station names, which changes lexical familiarity as well as language.

There are internal presentation inconsistencies that complicate verification. For example, the Appendix D discussion names a Doubao-415 comparison while Figure A3 is labeled with Doubao-428 and Doubao-115/428, and the surrounding prose contradicts itself about whether Augustins was identified as being on Line 18 or Line 12. These are correctable, but they weaken the qualitative evidence used to support a central claim.

strengths: The paper targets a useful and challenging capability: extracting and planning routes from high-resolution, information-dense transit maps. This combines OCR, visual grounding, and graph-like spatial reasoning in a practically understandable setting.

The dataset covers 30 cities in 13 countries, includes multilingual maps, and uses city-disjoint training and test sets. The short and long question formats probe both route selection and finer details such as intermediate-stop counts.

The evaluation spans 16 open- and closed-source MLLMs and includes text-only masking, symbolic-map inputs, difficulty breakdowns, error cases, and an RL training baseline. These provide more diagnostic value than reporting a single leaderboard.
The authors report manual correction and verification, including review by three domain experts, and transparently note an approximately 16% error rate before correction.
The manuscript is generally organized and readable, with clear templates, dataset statistics, algorithms, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central correctness metric does not validate the full requested answer. Algorithm 1 checks endpoints, line membership, and transfer consistency, but does not verify intermediate-stop identities or counts for long questions, route direction/order, or route optimality. Thus a response with incorrect long-form details can still be counted as fully correct. This materially undermines the principal accuracy tables and the claimed two-level evaluation framework.

The metric can accept suboptimal routes even though every prompt requests an “optimal route,” and optimality itself is never formally defined—fewest transfers, fewest stops, shortest time, or another criterion. Reference routes collected from live Google/Gaode services may also optimize criteria not represented by the static map.

The proposed map score has significant technical ambiguities. It pairs predicted and reference segments without specifying alignment when their numbers differ, treats via stops partly as sets and therefore ignores their order, and its normalized stop-count expression is undefined when both counts are zero. The pseudocode for clipping and correctness bonuses is also difficult to interpret. These are substantive metric-validity issues rather than presentation refinements.

The headline conclusion that open-source reasoning models underperform base models while closed-source reasoning models improve is not supported by controlled comparisons. Most entries are different model families, sizes, training recipes, API versions, and inference pipelines; only a limited subset resembles a direct base/reasoning comparison. No uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported, despite a test set of only 312 examples and just 23 hard examples.

The custom difficulty weighting is heuristic, and some difficulty cells contain only one example. Main conclusions rely on weighted results without adequately reporting uncertainty or establishing that the manually chosen weights reflect meaningful differences in task difficulty.

The RL study lacks an SFT baseline, making the claim that RL is needed because the evaluation metric is non-differentiable incorrect: supervised learning can still train on reference answers. Improvements may largely reflect format compliance, especially because the stated rewards are only correctness and format rewards. Training curves, variance across seeds, stopping criteria, and several implementation details are absent.

The description of GRPO is technically incomplete: the presented objective is essentially mean-centered policy gradient and omits important elements normally associated with GRPO, including variance normalization, importance-ratio clipping, and the stated KL regularization term. This weakens the technical correctness and reproducibility of the training contribution.

The dataset’s reliability is insufficiently documented. The paper reports that all errors found after an initial 16% error rate were corrected, but provides no inter-annotator agreement, independent post-correction audit, per-field error analysis, or released verification protocol. Difficulty labels and map selection also involve subjective manual decisions.

Several analyses overstate their evidence. The claim that failures mainly arise from grounding and spatial reasoning is based largely on selected cases and comparisons to separately reported OCRBench scores rather than controlled component-level tests. Likewise, interpreting a few within-family model results as confirmation of a scaling law is not justified.

Reproducibility remains uncertain: closed models use undocumented default API settings, exact image transformations and inference parameters are incomplete, RL training duration and hardware are not reported, and the ethics statement says copyrighted map images will not be redistributed. Reliance on external map links and mutable routing services may prevent reconstruction of the benchmark.

Overall, the transit-map benchmark has potential value, but the correctness and quality metrics do not reliably measure the requested route details or optimality. Because these metrics underpin nearly every quantitative claim, the current evidence does not adequately support acceptance.

strengths: REASONMAP targets an important and insufficiently studied capability: jointly reading dense, high-resolution visual maps and planning routes. Its 1,008 question-answer pairs cover 30 cities, 13 countries, multiple languages, and explicit map/question difficulty labels.

The dataset construction is thoughtful: routes are grounded in map-service results, visually checked against the displayed maps, and reviewed by three domain experts. The authors report finding and correcting an initial error rate of about 16%, which demonstrates meaningful quality control.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering 16 open- and closed-source MLLMs, short and detailed route questions, token usage, difficulty/city breakdowns, visual-masking tests, symbolic-map inputs, language analysis, metric sensitivity, and qualitative failure cases.

Separating route feasibility from similarity to reference routes is useful because more than one valid route can exist. The rule-based evaluator and structured output format should also make future model comparisons relatively inexpensive.

The visual-masking and symbolic-representation experiments provide convincing evidence that the benchmark is not solved purely through language priors. The low absolute results, including 63.02% short-question and 59.11% long-question accuracy for the strongest evaluated model, leave substantial headroom.
The cross-city reinforcement-fine-tuning experiment is a useful baseline: improvements are consistent for both model sizes and particularly large for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, while token use also decreases.
weaknesses: The correctness metric does not fully measure correctness of the requested long answers. Algorithm 1 checks route names, segment endpoints, and transfer consistency but ignores the predicted intermediate-stop list and intermediate-stop count; consequently, a long answer with incorrect requested details can still receive accuracy 1. These details affect only the separate map score, so the reported long-question accuracy is potentially misleading.

The route validator checks that both endpoints belong to each named line, but does not explicitly check their order, branch-level reachability, or whether the proposed service directly connects them. This can accept infeasible segments on branched transit lines. It also does not enforce optimality despite prompts requesting one optimal route.

The map-score specification has consequential ambiguities. Segment pairs are compared without defining alignment when predicted and reference routes contain different numbers of segments; the via-count expression can involve a zero denominator when both counts are zero; and Algorithm 2 uses slash notation for the short/long alternatives in a way that reads mathematically as division. These issues impede independent reproduction of the principal quality metric.

The headline conclusion that open-source reasoning models underperform base models while closed-source reasoning models show the opposite is confounded by heterogeneous model families, sizes, training data, APIs, and image preprocessing. Only Kimi provides a relatively direct open-source base/reasoning comparison, while o3 versus 4o is not a controlled reasoning-tuning ablation. The paper acknowledges part of this limitation, but its causal explanation based on visual grounding remains supported mainly by selected cases.

The GRPO evidence does not establish that reinforcement learning is preferable to simpler adaptation. The claim that supervised fine-tuning is insufficient because the evaluation metric is nondifferentiable is technically unconvincing: SFT can learn from reference outputs without differentiating through the metric. No SFT or format-only baseline, multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or training-duration details are reported, so the gains may partly reflect format learning or ordinary domain adaptation.

The custom difficulty weights are heuristic, and several evaluation strata are very small—the hard/medium bucket contains only one sample and city subsets range from 7 to 40 samples. Confidence intervals or significance tests are absent, weakening conclusions drawn from fine-grained comparisons and modest differences.

Reproducibility is only partial because the benchmark does not redistribute copyrighted map images and instead relies on source links. External maps may change or disappear, and the manuscript does not specify immutable versions, retrieval dates, or hashes that would guarantee identical visual inputs. Closed-model default API settings further limit exact replication.
